content.title: About
content.content: Tortellini are small ring-shaped pasta filled with creamy cheese. They are served with a smooth cream sauce that highlights the mild cheese flavor and makes the dish rich and satisfying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortellini originate from Italy; the name comes from the verb “torcere” meaning “to twist,” describing their shape.
Traditional fillings use ricotta, Parmesan, and sometimes spinach, while modern versions may include mozzarella, gorgonzola, or other cheeses.
Cream sauce is often made from heavy cream, butter, and Parmesan, occasionally enriched with white wine or aromatic herbs.
Tortellini are a popular festive dish because they look elegant and are easy to prepare in large quantities.
In Italy there is a regional variant called “tortellini in broth,” where the pasta is served in a light meat broth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The cheese filling provides a good source of complete protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheeses used in the filling contain calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tortellini, like most pasta, supplies B1, B2 and B3 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy‑dense cream sauce
items.content: Cream and butter add concentrated calories, useful for people with high energy needs.

items.title: Potential probiotic content
items.content: If fermented cheeses are used, they may contribute beneficial bacteria for gut health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese and cream contain lactose, so those who are intolerant should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein may react to the cheese filling.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and cheese make the dish calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Cheeses are often salty, which can increase sodium intake—caution for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional tortellini are made from wheat flour, making them unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tortellini hot, drizzled with cream sauce. Garnish with grated Parmesan, fresh herbs (basil, parsley) and a light salad. For a lighter option, use a yogurt‑based or plant‑based cream sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Dry tortellini keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months. Fresh filled tortellini store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 2 months.
